open_obligations: Check Khan et al.'s exact recommendation and whether they claimed an accuracy gain from both orders
Account for the different single-order baselines (Khan et al. always put the correct answer first, per private communication)
in.other_title: Kenton et al. find Khan et al.'s both-orders judging gives no accuracy gain over randomised order
in.rationale: The authors confirm judge positional bias but find Khan et al.'s recommended remedy does not change mean accuracy. The setting differs: the authors regenerate debates for the reversed order and randomise the correct position, while Khan et al. swapped presentation of the same debates (footnote 2). The citing passage names the cited work; the target is the cited paper's main record, not a record of the specific result.
in.scope: proposed CHALLENGES: Whether judging in both answer orders improves mean judge accuracy relative to a randomised single order

open_obligations: Check Khan et al.'s Fig 31 to confirm it shows debate below or equal to direct QA with a same-model judge
Check that the datasets behind Khan et al.'s Fig 31 lack information asymmetry like the authors' closed tasks
in.other_title: Kenton et al.: with judge equal to debaters, debate trails direct QA, similar to Khan et al. Fig 31
in.rationale: Khan et al. report limited results on non-QuALITY datasets with a same-model judge where debate does not beat standard QA; the authors explicitly describe their Pro 1.5 result as similar. No dedicated record exists for this Khan finding, so the CORE record is used. The citing passage names the cited work; the target is the cited paper's main record, not a record of the specific result.
in.scope: proposed SUPPORTS: Debate vs direct QA when there is no information asymmetry and no judge-debater capability gap

open_obligations: Check Khan et al.'s Fig. 20 shows no accuracy gain with more debate rounds
Confirm both studies vary rounds within a comparable range (1 to 3)
in.other_title: Kenton et al. find more debate turns do not help weak judges, consistent with Khan et al. on QuALITY
in.rationale: The authors explicitly say their turn ablation is consistent with Khan et al., who (per the authors' Appendix F.1) saw no improvement with number of rounds on QuALITY. No Khan record covers rounds, so CORE is used. The citing passage names the cited work; the target is the cited paper's main record, not a record of the specific result.
in.scope: proposed SUPPORTS: Effect of the number of debate/consultancy turns on judge accuracy

open_obligations: Locate Khan et al.'s turn-count comparison (three-round vs one-round) and check that it used comparable judges
Check that Arnesen et al.'s one-turn models were trained with the same procedure as the two-turn models (Appendix G says identical procedures)
in.other_title: Arnesen et al. find one- and two-turn debates are judged equally well, as Khan et al. observed
in.rationale: An explicit 'aligns with the findings of' statement. No record of Khan et al.'s paper states the turn-count result, so the link is paper-level; Arnesen et al. describe it (p19 L36-37) as Khan et al. not seeing higher accuracy in three-round than in one-round debates. The citing passage names the cited work; the target is the cited paper's main record, not a record of the specific result.
in.scope: proposed SUPPORTS: Effect of the number of debate turns on judge accuracy; holds for LLM-judged QuALITY debates

open_obligations: Check that the authors' own results show gains over the solo-verifier baseline (p9 L48-L55) of a kind comparable to Khan et al.'s judge-accuracy gains
Note that the authors do not test whether stronger provers help more, which is the capability part of Khan et al.'s claim
in.other_title: Hammond et al.'s neural interactive proofs tentatively support Khan et al. on oversight viability
in.rationale: The authors explicitly place their findings (modest accuracy gains over a solo verifier, larger worst-case gains) alongside Khan et al.'s debate results as evidence pointing the same way, which is SUPPORTS. Settings differ: Khan et al. use inference-time debate on QuALITY reading comprehension with an information asymmetry, the authors train verifiers on code validation.
in.scope: proposed SUPPORTS: Whether interaction with stronger models helps a weaker judge or verifier; the agreement is tentative and holds at the level of overall direction, not specific accuracy numbers

open_obligations: Check that Khan et al. (2024) use QuALITY and a fixed-round, non-recursive debate protocol
Note that the critique is collective; confirm nothing in the passage singles out Khan et al.
in.other_title: Buhl et al. say evidence like Khan et al.'s QuALITY debate results is too limited for a safety case
in.rationale: The authors characterise prior empirical work, including Khan et al., as limited in dataset and protocol depth, a scope critique without new data. The critique is made collectively about five studies, so it applies to Khan et al. only as one member of that group.
in.scope: proposed CRITIQUES: Whether existing empirical debate results support the safety case's claims; holds as a critique of scope (dataset, recursion depth), not of the reported accuracy gains

open_obligations: Check that Khan et al.'s QuALITY judges indeed had no relevant prior beliefs about the fictional stories, which is what makes the omission a scope limit rather than an error

in.other_title: Rahman et al. say Khan et al.'s debate evaluation does not consider judges' prior beliefs
in.rationale: The passage names a limitation of how the cited work evaluated debate (no account of judges' prior beliefs) rather than reporting a conflicting result, so CRITIQUES. No Khan et al. record states this limitation, so the core claim is the target. The citing passage names the cited work; the target is the cited paper's main record, not a record of the specific result.
in.scope: proposed CRITIQUES: Whether debate's measured benefit for judges holds when judges bring strong prior beliefs; Khan et al.'s reading-comprehension setting has no such priors

text: The authors report that on the QuALITY comprehension task, debate between two LLM experts who can read the story helps non-expert judges who cannot, with non-expert LLM judges reaching 76% and human judges 88% accuracy versus naive baselines of 48% and 60%. They further report that optimising expert debaters for persuasiveness in an unsupervised manner (judge approval, no ground-truth labels) improves the non-expert's ability to identify the truth in debates.
title: Debate helps non-expert LLM and human judges on QuALITY; persuasive debaters help more
